newsitem.title: USA: Miami mayor's budget would not raise garbage fees.
newsitem.headline: Miami mayor's budget would not raise garbage fees.

text.p: Miami Mayor Joe Carollo laid out a budget plan Thursday that uses wage and pension concessions, grants, cost cuts and fee hikes to balance the city budget without raising property taxes or garbage fees or selling valuable land.

The plan consists of $17.57 million of new one-time revenues, $15.76 million of recurring new revenues and $37.8 million of recurring savings, which Carollo said would more than offset the city's $68 million deficit for the year that began Oct 1.
"I've been very conservative. Most of the numbers that I've put down have been well below the expected savings or revenues," Carollo told the city commission.

Included in the one-time revenues is a $12.6 million grant to the city from the Miami Sports and Exhibition Authority, which runs the Miami Arena. Carollo did not explain what, if anything that money had previously been earmarked for but said the authority had already agreed to give it to the city.
His plan assumes the city will collect at least $3 million of the $7 million it is owed in delinquent garbage fees, and lists that revenue as recurring.

Carollo said the federal government has also agreed to give the city $6 million in grants for extra police officers and equipment, and to waive the $3 million matching fee the city otherwise would have had to pay.
"This is a very solid grant that we will have no trouble receiving again," Police Chief Donald Warshaw said.

Carollo listed much of the police grant money in his budget as "recurring revenues." Firefighters' union spokesman Shorty Bryson questioned that, noting the grants were only guaranteed for this year and next.
"I believe that the grants are ticking time bombs," Bryson said. "I do not look at grants as recurring revenues. We need to find more recurring revenue that's real."

Carollo also listed as recurring revenues $5.3 million in management pension concessions and more than $12 million in union wage concessions, even though the latter have only been pledged for this year and next.

Three of the city's four unions have approved them, but that approval was contingent on doubling garbage fees, which would raise $10 million in new revenue and end general fund subsidization of city garbage services.
Carollo and two of the other four city commissioners vehemently oppose a garbage fee hike, saying it would put an unbearable burden in Miami's poor residents.

Doubling the garbage fees was a crucial component of the bail-out plan drafted by interim city manager Merrett Stierheim and has strongly been urged by rating agencies, which have already lowered Miami's bond rating to non-investment grade.

But the mayor said his plan left open the possibility of privatizing the garbage department in 1999. That provoked immediate, angry reaction and accusations of racism from the sanitation workers' union, whose predominantly black members were hardest hit in the city's last round of job-cutting.

Carollo said his plan would give the city "breathing room," to seek other new revenue sources and expand its property tax base. He said there was "no doubt in my mind" that new construction now under way or in the planning stages would bring in enough new ad valorem revenue to take up the slack.

The mayor had previously discussed selling city property, including a valuable waterfront parcel, to raise cash. His plan does not call for "even one inch" or property to be sold. Carollo said the city may still consider that, but only if it was a good deal for the city and "not because we have to."
The city commission plans to vote on final budget revisions on December 23, and must submit their budget to the state emergency oversight board by January 3.

About $5 million of the new or increased fees included in his budget have already been approved by the commission. The panel voted Thursday to raise building inspection fees and dockage fees at city marinas, and set up a mechanism to collect fire district fees if such fees are adopted later.
